source.version_note: European Journal of Social Psychology 53:779–804 (2023), accepted 12 January 2023. Seven controlled samples plus one aggregate public-web survey are reported; the abstract's total N=3752 excludes the large public survey.
source.verification_method: All 26 supplied pages read, including all study designs, contrasts, tables, internal meta-analyses, footnotes and references. Supplemental appendices are not embedded in the supplied file.

citation.title: Innocence over utilitarianism: Heightened moral standards for robots in rescue dilemmas

reading.source_scope_note: Human judgments about hypothetical human or robot lifeguards choosing whom to rescue. Number, culpability, social status and robot descriptions vary. No deployed rescue algorithm, actual rescue, punishment behavior or identified machine moral capacity.
access_limits: All 26 supplied pages read, including studies 1, 2a–2c, 3, 4a–4b and 5 and their internal meta-analyses.

OSF raw datasets, scripts, preregistrations and Appendices A–F were not independently inspected. Supplementary outcomes and simulation-based sensitivity results are described but not claimed fully reproduced. Cited original psychology studies and books remain unread.

study.controlled_samples: Study 1 N=216 in text/gender counts, versus 217 in Table 1; 2a N=186 after 27 exclusions from 213; 2b N=266; 2c N=446 after 57 of 503 excluded; 4a N=912 of 1000; 4b N=811 of 958; 5 N=915 of 1001. Text sample sizes sum to 3752 across seven controlled samples, not eight controlled experiments plus the web sample.
study.study_1_to_2b: Between-person human/drone/android by rescue one innocent fisherman or two culpable intoxicated motorboaters. Studies 2a/2b swap descriptions of cognitive autonomy between drone and android across separate samples.
study.study_2c: Between-person agent by rescued party by motorboater socioeconomic status; one person in each party, removing the number tradeoff. Strong culpability contrast, small status-by-decision effect, no detected agent-by-decision interaction.
study.study_3: Open Finnish public broadcaster survey. Fixed-order culpable-versus-mechanical-accident scenarios; participants can skip questions. Four question-specific Ns: 19315, 19195, 18533, 18383. Only aggregate distributions available, with unknown overlap and no human agent condition.
study.study_4: 4a preregistered English-speaking multinational sample and 4b Czech replication: human/android and culpable fisherman/motorboaters between person; each participant rates both rescue decisions in counterbalanced order. Seven judgment items collected, mainly acceptability/wrongness reported here.
study.study_5: Preregistered human/android by all-culpable/all-innocent, with two rescue ratings per person. When culpability is matched, saving two is generally preferred; choosing one is more strongly penalized for robots. Some unexpectedly lower approval for rescuing an innocent fisherman is exploratory.
study.meta_analysis: Internal fixed-effect estimates show a small overall robot disadvantage, Hedges g=−.17. Rescue-culpable contrast g=−.29 versus innocent g=−.06 (undetected); norm/agent moderation varies with fixed versus mixed-effects specification. Multiple experiments and this internal synthesis remain one paper.

summary: Add folk justice as the article's explicit descriptive construct of desert/innocence-based judgment. Extend existing agent-asymmetry and anthropomorphism evidence with conditional effects, nulls and competing norms. Preserve the distinction between intuitions about culpability and an ethically justified rescue policy.

findings.definition: Intuitive judgments about what people deserve in light of their perceived innocence or culpability.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human evaluation pattern tested across hypothetical rescue dilemmas with described AI/robot agents; not a validated ethical rule or actual robot decision process
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether descriptions of a person's fault or social status cause an AI-assisted allocation to discount their interests beyond authorized, relevant criteria. Separate causal responsibility, deserved punishment, protection of others and equal rights; document the effect without turning popularity or culpability into permission to deny care or rescue.
findings.novelty_rationale: A descriptive desert-related concern about the recipient of help, distinct from judging the decision-maker's character or assuming existing outcomes are deserved. The authors explicitly use folk justice to avoid deciding whether protecting innocence or punishing guilt is the operative motive.

findings.evidence_scope: The rescue scenarios contrast numbers saved with fault for the accident, later independently varying or matching culpability. Participants generally favor rescuing the innocent when this conflicts with saving two culpable people; robot penalties depend on which norm is violated. The separate protective-versus-punitive motive is not directly measured.
findings.boundary: Perceived culpability is not adjudicated responsibility, diminished human worth or a general loss of a right to rescue. A preference can be unfair or mistaken, and desert considerations can be relevant in some contexts without justifying every allocation. Do not infer machine moral feeling, a universal utilitarian calculus or permission to punish through withholding rescue.

findings.definition: The relative evaluation of human and robotic rescuers depends on whether the rescue decision violates the moral concern salient in the described scenario.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing agent-asymmetry entry receives another fully read paper; a larger penalty for some bad decisions is not a separate universal mechanism or several independent citations.

findings.evidence_scope: Controlled experiments and within-paper synthesis show conditional robot penalties, including useful nonreplications and differences by outcome. Both source types generally follow similar preference directions. In the large web survey, no human source is included, so it does not test agent asymmetry.
findings.boundary: A larger robot penalty is not automatically an irrational double standard: professional role, controllability, expected competence and perceived risk may matter. Population agreement does not establish an objectively good/bad action. Undetected contrasts are not equivalence, and distinct judgment scales are not interchangeable.

findings.term: Anthropomorphism effects vary by decision and described autonomy
findings.definition: Human-like appearance and cognitive-autonomy descriptions can alter expectations and evaluation of a robotic rescuer, without a uniform benefit for every decision.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing human-attribution concept; do not create independent smart-drone and android biases from crossed descriptions across separate studies.

findings.evidence_scope: Studies 2a/2b describe drone/android and programmed/independent capacities in different pairings. Some stronger penalties occur for human-like or independent robots, particularly for norm violations. This is not a continuous visual uncanny-valley test or an isolated fully crossed within-sample mechanism test.
findings.boundary: Appearance, attributed mind, actual autonomy and mental experience differ. Human-like framing may improve or worsen specific judgments. No measured threat, eeriness or empathy mediator explains every result; source descriptions do not establish a robot's feelings or actual capabilities.

findings.term: Rescue preference is distinct from an omission preference
findings.definition: When both offered responses are active rescue choices, their contrast does not directly measure preference for doing nothing.
findings.novelty_rationale: Clarify an existing construct rather than count every non-utilitarian choice as omission bias or deontology.
findings.evidence_scope: All main rescue options require selecting and helping one party. This reduces the usual action/inaction confound, but the study does not independently manipulate omission or identify all reasons for the agent difference.
findings.boundary: Both rescue options still leave someone unaided; the offered-action design does not settle every philosophical distinction between causing and allowing harm. No new empirical omission effect or causal explanation is claimed.

findings.term: Judging a recipient's desert differs from judging an actor's character
findings.definition: Information about the person who may receive help can shape evaluation of another person's decision without manipulating the rescuer's own character.
findings.novelty_rationale: Boundary clarification linking the new folk-justice entry to an existing character-based judgment entry, without treating patient and agent character as identical manipulations.

findings.evidence_scope: Culpability and status vary for fisherman/motorboaters, not the lifeguard's own prior moral conduct. The source explicitly calls attention to this distinction.
findings.boundary: Victim fault, stable character, legal entitlement, actor intent and rescue priority are separate variables. Do not fill the actor-character bibliography gap with a different patient-character manipulation.

methodological_limits: The total 3752 sums the seven controlled sample sizes in the text; the eighth study is the separate open web survey. Do not add four question-specific web Ns as unique people or describe all eight studies as randomized experiments.

Study 1 N=216 in text and demographic counts, but Table 1 says 217. Its interaction effect size also differs between prose and Table 2. The supplied numbers are preserved as inconsistent; no corrected participant count or effect size is invented.

Studies 1–2b confound rescuing two with rescuing the culpable, and one with the innocent. Later studies help separate these variables, but early main effects cannot independently identify number and culpability weights.

Folk justice deliberately combines protecting innocence and punishing wrongdoing. The authors do not directly ask motives. Study 5 gives an indirect reason to favor the protection account but does not uniquely identify it.

Drunkenness, reckless steering, causing an accident and responsibility cues are bundled. Social status manipulation uses a label; moral judgments can reflect sympathy, need, perceived risk or stereotypes rather than a single desert mechanism.

Culpability manipulations describe facts rather than an adjudicated legal status, and the setting limits rescue to one party. Results do not establish real triage protocols or ethically justify denying rescue as punishment.

Robot form and cognitive independence are bundled within each of Studies 2a/2b and swapped across separate samples. This does not fully cross all components in one randomized sample or distinguish appearance from every cohort difference.

The experiments are text descriptions rather than live robots or a continuum of visual human-likeness. Calling the pattern uncanny-valley moderation does not establish an actual U-shaped curve, eeriness response or identity-threat mediator.
Study 2c does not detect an agent-by-decision effect, and one exploratory high-status contrast is p=.053. Do not promote it to significance or erase this nonreplication from the evidence trail.

The public survey has no randomization, no human agent, fixed vignette order, optional missing answers and unknown identity overlap. Independent-sample Welch tests ignore overlap; random pairing simulations do not recover actual within-person covariance or remove selection/order effects.

Study 3 prints Welch df=41864 for the pure-accident comparison, exceeding the maximum N1+N2−2=36914 implied by its listed 18533 and 18383 responses. Actual response totals/statistics require reconciliation; corrected values are not guessed.

Study 2a prints interaction F(1,180)=3.21, p=.042 for a three-level agent factor, for which numerator df=2 would ordinarily apply. Its android contrast B=−.72 has a printed interval [−1.28,+.16] despite p=.012. Study 2b's human contrast coefficient and interval signs also need reconciliation.

Mixed/repeated-study reported df range near N and near 2N, with Satterthwaite corrections referenced but exact random-effect specification unavailable here. Some displayed partial eta-squared values do not reconcile with the printed F/df. Code and original output are needed before declaring a precise correction or inferring effective independent sample size.

Study 5's concluding paragraph says a pattern holds when the robot rescues two, while the immediately preceding contrasts locate the extra robot penalty in rescuing one. Preserve the numerical contrasts and flag this apparent direction-of-action wording error.

Seven judgment items plus exploratory outcomes are collected in later studies; main text reports mainly acceptability/wrongness and directs others to supplements. Preregistration is reported for 4a and 5, but not independently verified here. Omitted scales are not assumed identical or fabricated.

Several planned and exploratory contrasts have nominal p-values. Small or borderline subgroup effects need their disclosed status and appropriate familywise interpretation; a within-paper meta-analysis does not supply independent replication beyond these studies.

Internal meta-analyses collapse robot types, combine related contrasts and use fixed-effect and mixed-effect specifications. Dependence among effects sharing a sample must be modeled. The agent-by-folk-justice interaction loses significance under the reported mixed-effect alternative, so its precision is model-sensitive.

Common-direction normative preferences do not prove identical decision processes across humans and robots. An undetected norm-abiding agent contrast is not an equivalence test or proof of universally equal evaluation.

The power analyses emphasize main effects or targeted pairwise contrasts, while some early interactions have low sensitivity. Decomposing a difficult interaction into powered contrasts does not automatically establish every higher-order interaction.

Exclusions use attention/manipulation checks and, in later samples, health/fluency restrictions. A yes/yes response to making one's own shoes/clothes is treated as implausible despite possible genuine craftspeople; no sensitivity to that rule is reproduced. An implausible age response is excluded only from age summaries as disclosed.

Finnish library/university samples, English-speaking Prolific users and Czech volunteers broaden coverage but do not represent all cultures, disabled people or real rescuers. Compensation/recruitment and scenario setting differ across samples.

Expected rationality, lack of robot emotion, empathizing with human decision-makers, physical risk and need for a robot to justify its use are competing proposed explanations. None is causally isolated in these experiments.

One article with multiple studies and internal synthesis remains one research-paper citation. Its primary citations, books, supplementary measurements and public individual-level records are not claimed independently read or reproduced.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The driving paper finds a largely general human action-rating advantage; the current rescue paper finds stronger decision-dependent penalties. Context, patient culpability, action set and human-like manipulation differ, so neither establishes a universal agent rule.

Nursing judgments bundle coercion, authority and patient autonomy; the present agent acts without an explicit order. This removes one obedience cue without proving chain-of-command is the sole cause of differences across papers.

Both studies emphasize that the recipient of an action matters. Robot experience attribution in a patient role and a human recipient's culpability are different manipulations and should not fill each other's evidence gaps.
A contextual nursing null and a rescue penalty are compatible with heterogeneous evaluations. Stakes and human-likeness remain proposed moderators unless directly compared in a common design.

deferred.reason: A contextual description of the existing human–robot judgment asymmetry, not a separate independent behavior from the same evidence.
The study does not distinguish punishment motives from protecting innocence or observe actual withholding. Folk justice is the authors' deliberately neutral umbrella.
Culpability/recipient deservingness is captured by the new folk-justice entry and linked to existing actor-character judgment rather than double-counted as a near-synonymous behavior.

limitations: One descriptive moral-judgment construct added. Normative rights, actual rescue authority and causal mechanisms are not inferred, and no automatic violation/harm edges are added.
